title: Parts of Speech
notes: What Are Parts of Speech?

Parts of Speech are the categories into which words are classified based on their function in a sentence. English has eight traditional parts of speech: noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection. A word may belong to different parts of speech depending on how it is used in a particular sentence. For example, 'run' can be a verb ('I run every day') or a noun ('That was a good run').
Noun: Definition and Types

A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing, idea, or quality. Nouns are classified into several types: Proper Nouns name specific individuals or places (e.g., Kathmandu, Sita, Nepal) and are always capitalised. Common Nouns name general items (e.g., city, girl, country). Collective Nouns refer to a group considered as a whole (e.g., team, herd, committee). Material Nouns name substances (e.g., gold, water, wood). Abstract Nouns name ideas or qualities (e.g., honesty, bravery, freedom). Countable Nouns can be counted and have plural forms; Uncountable Nouns cannot be counted and take singular verbs.
Pronoun: Types and Uses

A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun to avoid repetition. Personal Pronouns refer to specific people or things: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (and their objective forms: me, him, her, us, them). Reflective Pronouns end in -self/-selves and are used when the subject and object are the same (e.g., 'She taught herself'). Relative Pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, that) connect clauses to nouns. Demonstrative Pronouns (this, that, these, those) point to specific things. Indefinite Pronouns (some, any, none, all, each, either, neither) refer to non-specific entities. Interrogative Pronouns (who, whom, which, what) are used to ask questions.
Verb: Action and State

A verb is the most important part of speech — it expresses action or state of being. Action Verbs show physical or mental activity (e.g., run, think, write). State Verbs (also called stative verbs) describe conditions rather than actions (e.g., be, seem, belong, know). Transitive Verbs require a direct object (e.g., 'She kicked the ball'). Intransitive Verbs do not take an object (e.g., 'He slept'). Linking Verbs (be, seem, become, appear) connect the subject to a complement. Auxiliary (Helping) Verbs (be, do, have) combine with main verbs to form tenses, voices, and moods.
Adjective: Describing Nouns

An adjective modifies or describes a noun or pronoun, providing more information about its quality, quantity, or identity. Descriptive Adjectives describe qualities (e.g., beautiful, tall, intelligent). Demonstrative Adjectives (this, that, these, those) identify specific nouns. Quantitative Adjectives (some, many, few, little, enough) indicate quantity. Numeral Adjectives (one, first, double) indicate number or order. Possessive Adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) show ownership. Interrogative Adjectives (which, what, whose) modify nouns in questions. Adjectives generally precede the noun they modify ('a red car'), but some follow linking verbs ('The sky is blue').
Adverb: Modifying More Than Verbs

An adverb modifies verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or even entire sentences. It answers questions such as how?, when?, where?, why?, to what extent? Adverbs of Manner describe how something happens (e.g., quickly, carefully, well). Adverbs of Time (now, yesterday, soon) indicate when. Adverbs of Place (here, there, everywhere) indicate where. Adverbs of Frequency (always, often, never) indicate how often. Adverbs of Degree (very, too, almost, quite) indicate intensity. Many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to adjectives, but important exceptions exist: fast (not 'fastly'), hard vs. hardly (different meanings), late vs. lately.
Preposition: Showing Relationships

A preposition shows the relationship between a noun (or pronoun) and another word in the sentence. Prepositions commonly indicate place (at, in, on, under, above, between), time (at, on, in, before, after, during), and direction (to, into, towards, through). Common prepositions include: at (specific time/place), in (enclosed spaces, months, years), on (surfaces, days), by (agent, near), with (accompaniment), from (origin), about (concerning). A prepositional phrase consists of a preposition plus its object (e.g., 'in the morning', 'on the table').
Conjunction: Joining Elements

A conjunction connects words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating Conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equal elements. Subordinating Conjunctions (because, although, if, when, while, since, unless, once, before, after) join a dependent clause to an independent clause. Correlative Conjunctions work in pairs: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or. The position of a conjunction matters — 'I stayed because it was raining' differs from 'Because it was raining, I stayed' in emphasis but not meaning.
Article: The Indefinite Article

The indefinite articles a and an are used before singular, countable nouns when referring to something non-specific. Use a before consonant sounds (not just letters): 'a university' (yoo-niversity), 'a one-way street' (won-way). Use an before vowel sounds: 'an hour' (the h is silent), 'an MBA degree'. Articles are one of the most frequently misused elements by NEB students, especially in written passages and error correction exercises.
Article: The Definite Article

The definite article the is used before nouns that are specific or already known to the reader. Use 'the' when: the noun has been mentioned before ('I saw a dog. The dog was black'); there is only one of something ('The sun rises in the east'); superlatives and ordinals ('the best', 'the first'); rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, plural country names ('the Himalaya', 'the USA'); and musical instruments ('play the guitar'). No article is used before: generic plurals ('Dogs are loyal'), names of meals ('have breakfast'), most proper nouns ('Kathmandu is beautiful'), abstract nouns in general sense ('Honesty is the best policy'), and languages ('I study English').
Modals: Helping Verbs with Special Meaning

Modal verbs (also called modal auxiliaries) express necessity, possibility, permission, ability, or advice. The primary modals are: can (ability, permission), could (past ability, polite request), may (permission, possibility), might (remote possibility), shall (formal future, suggestions), should (advice, obligation), will (future, willingness), would (conditional, polite request), must (strong obligation, deduction). Semi-modals include ought to (moral duty), need (necessity), have to (external obligation). Modals are followed by the base form of the main verb (without 'to', except 'ought to' and 'have to'). Modals do not change form for person or number, and they do not take -s, -ing, or -ed endings.
Non-finite Verbs: Infinitives, Gerunds, and Participles

Non-finite verbs are verb forms that do not show tense or agree with a subject. There are three types: Infinitives (to + base verb) function as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs ('I want to go', 'the book to read', 'I called to inform you'). Gerunds (verb + -ing functioning as a noun) serve as subjects, objects, or complements ('Swimming is fun', 'I enjoy reading'). Participles have two forms: the Past Participle (usually -ed or -en) functions as an adjective or in perfect tenses ('the broken window'); the Present Participle (-ing form) functions as an adjective, in continuous tenses, or as an adverbial ('a crying baby', 'She ran, panting').
Gerund vs. Infinitive: Common Confusion Points

Some verbs are followed by gerunds, others by infinitives, and some by both with a change in meaning. Verbs followed by gerunds: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, practice, consider, suggest, admit, deny, imagine. Verbs followed by infinitives: want, decide, hope, plan, learn, agree, refuse, offer, promise, pretend. Verbs followed by both with different meanings: stop (stop doing = quit an activity vs. stop to do = pause in order to do), remember (remember doing = recall a past event vs. remember to do = not forget a task), forget (forget doing = fail to recall vs. forget to do = neglect to do), try (try doing = experiment vs. try to do = make an effort).
Subject-Verb Agreement: Core Principles

Subject-verb agreement means the verb must match its subject in number (singular or plural). Basic rules: (1) A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. (2) Collective nouns (team, class, government) usually take singular verbs when the group acts as one unit, but plural when members act individually. (3) Subjects joined by and usually take plural verbs ('Ravi and Sita are here'). (4) Subjects joined by or/nor take verbs that agree with the nearer subject ('Neither the teacher nor the students were present'). (5) 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither' before a singular noun take singular verbs ('Each of the boys has a pen'). (6) Indefinite pronouns like everyone, somebody, nobody take singular verbs ('Everyone is present').
Agreement with Tricky Subjects

Several subjects cause persistent agreement errors. Amounts of money, distance, time as a single quantity take singular verbs ('Ten rupees is too much', 'Two kilometres is a long walk'). The number vs. a number: 'The number of students is increasing' (singular) vs. 'A number of students are absent' (plural). Neither...nor, either...or, not only...but also: the verb agrees with the nearer subject. There is/are: the verb agrees with the subject that follows ('There is a book' vs. 'There are books'). One of the + plural noun + relative clause: the relative verb agrees with 'one' ('She is one of the students who study hard' — plural, because 'who' refers to 'students').
Determiners: Before Nouns

Determiners are words placed before nouns to specify or quantify them. They include: Articles (a, an, the). Demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Possessives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their). Quantifiers (some, any, many, much, few, little, several, all, both, each, every, either, neither). Numbers (one, two, first, second). Interrogatives (which, what, whose). Key distinction: few means 'not many' (negative connotation); a few means 'some' (positive connotation). little vs. a little follows the same pattern for uncountable nouns. fewer is used with countable nouns; less with uncountable nouns.
Prepositions: Common Error Patterns

Prepositions are among the most error-prone areas in English. Common pairs tested in NEB exams: at (specific points: at the door, at 5 PM), in (enclosed areas, larger places: in the room, in Kathmandu), on (surfaces, contact: on the table, on the wall). By indicates method or agent (written by me, by bus); with indicates accompaniment or instrument (go with him, cut with a knife). Among is used for three or more items; between for two items. Into indicates movement; in indicates position. Apart from means 'except' or 'in addition to'; besides means 'in addition to'. Students should practice common prepositional collocations: angry with a person, angry about a situation; good at (skill), good for (beneficial).
Conjunctions: Structure and Punctuation

Correct use of conjunctions requires attention to punctuation. When a coordinating conjunction joins two independent clauses, a comma precedes it: 'I wanted to go, but I was too tired.' When joining only two verbs or two objects, no comma is needed: 'I ran and jumped.' Subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses. When the dependent clause comes first, use a comma: 'Although it rained, we went out.' When it comes second, no comma is needed: 'We went out although it rained.' Correlative conjunctions require parallel structure: not only the teacher but also the students were happy (not 'was').
Parsing: Identifying All Parts of Speech

Parsing is the practice of identifying the part of speech, function, and grammatical properties of each word in a sentence. This skill is directly tested in NEB exams. For example, parsing the sentence 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog': The — definite article; quick — adjective (describing fox); brown — adjective (describing fox); fox — proper/common noun (subject); jumps — transitive verb (present simple, third person singular); over — preposition; the — definite article; lazy — adjective; dog — common noun (object of preposition). Always identify whether each noun is singular/plural, whether each verb shows tense and voice, and whether each adjective is in positive/comparative/superlative degree.

confusion: Who vs. Whom: 'Who' is a subject pronoun used when the person is doing the action (Who called you?); 'Whom' is an object pronoun used when the person receives the action (To whom did you speak?). In modern spoken English, 'whom' is often replaced by 'who', but in formal writing and NEB exams, distinguish them carefully.

Few vs. A few: 'Few' (without article) means 'not many' and has a negative connotation (I have few friends = almost no friends). 'A few' means 'some' and has a positive connotation (I have a few friends = some friends exist). The same distinction applies to 'little' vs. 'a little' with uncountable nouns.

Make vs. Do: 'Make' is used when creating or producing something concrete (make a cake, make a decision, make a mistake). 'Do' is used for actions, duties, and activities (do homework, do exercise, do the washing up). This distinction is frequently tested in error correction questions.

Less vs. Fewer: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns (fewer books, fewer students). 'Less' is used with uncountable nouns (less water, less time). However, 'less' is used with expressions of time, money, and distance as single quantities (less than 5 minutes, less than $10).

Say vs. Tell: 'Tell' requires a direct object (tell someone something: tell me the truth). 'Say' does not require a direct object (say something: say hello, she said that she was tired). We 'tell a story' but 'say a word'. In reported speech, 'tell' is used with an indirect object.

Its vs. It's: 'Its' (no apostrophe) is the possessive form of 'it' (the dog wagged its tail). 'It's' (with apostrophe) is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has' (it's raining, it's been a long day). This is one of the most common spelling errors in NEB writing sections.

Than vs. Then: 'Than' is used in comparisons (better than, more than, other than). 'Then' refers to time (then we went home) or sequence (first this, then that). Confusing these two is a frequent error in both writing and gap-fill exercises.

Affect vs. Effect: 'Affect' is primarily a verb meaning 'to influence' (The weather affects my mood). 'Effect' is primarily a noun meaning 'the result' (The effect was immediate). Note: 'effect' can also be a verb meaning 'to bring about' (to effect change), and 'affect' can be a noun in psychology (emotional affect).

Whoever vs. Whomever: 'Whoever' is used as a subject (Whoever arrives first will win). 'Whomever' is used as an object (Give the prize to whomever you choose). Test by replacing with 'he' (whoever) or 'him' (whomever).

Since vs. For: 'Since' is used with a specific point in time (since Monday, since 1990, since I was a child). 'For' is used with a duration of time (for three days, for two years, for a long time). Both can be used with the present perfect tense.
practice: Identify the parts of speech of each word in the sentence: 'The brilliant scientist carefully examined the mysterious specimen.' [Answer: The=article, brilliant=adjective, scientist=noun, carefully=adverb, examined=verb, the=article, mysterious=adjective, specimen=noun]
Choose the correct option: She has ___ friends in this city. (a) few (b) a few. Explain your choice. [Answer: (b) 'a few' — the sentence suggests she has some friends, a positive meaning.]

Correct the error in subject-verb agreement: Neither the boys nor the girl ___ coming to the party. (a) is (b) are [Answer: (a) 'is' — with 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the girl' (singular).]
Change the part of speech: Complete the table for the word 'decide': noun = ___, adjective = ___, adverb = ___. [Answer: noun = decision, adjective = decisive/decided, adverb = decisively]

Fill in the correct article (a/an/the or no article): ___ Ganges is a sacred river in India. ___ honesty is the best policy. He is ___ M.A. in English. I went to ___ school by ___ bus. [Answer: The Ganges; (no article) honesty; an M.A.; (no article) school; (no article) bus]
Choose the correct preposition: She is angry ___ her brother. He is good ___ mathematics. She went ___ Tokyo yesterday. [Answer: angry with; good at; went to]

Identify the type of pronoun used in each sentence: (a) She hurt herself. (b) Give the book to whoever comes first. (c) Neither of the boys has passed. (d) Someone left a message. [Answer: (a) reflexive, (b) interrogative/relative, (c) indefinite, (d) indefinite]

Differentiate between gerund and infinitive: Complete with the correct form: I enjoy ___ (read) novels. I want ___ (visit) Kathmandu. I stopped ___ (smoke) last year. I forgot ___ (lock) the door. [Answer: reading, to visit, smoking (quit the habit), to lock (didn't do the task)]

Choose the correct form: This is the house ___ I was born. (a) which (b) where (c) that (d) in which. [Answer: All of (b), (c), and (d) are correct. 'Where' = relative adverb; 'in which' is the formal equivalent.]

Rewrite using the correct comparative/superlative form: This is the ___ (good) book I have ever read. Of the two brothers, Ram is the ___ (tall) one. [Answer: best, taller (comparative used with 'of the two')]
universalFacts: The concept of parts of speech originated with ancient Greek grammarians, particularly Dionysius Thrax (2nd century BCE), who classified words into eight categories. This system was later adopted by Latin grammarians and passed down through the Western tradition.

In Nepali, the concept of parts of speech (पद वर्ग) is similarly structured but includes additional categories specific to the language, such as अव्यय (indeclinables). Understanding both systems helps NEB students grasp grammatical concepts more deeply.

The eight-part classification system is somewhat arbitrary — modern linguistics recognises additional categories like determiners (a, the, this, some) as a separate class from adjectives, and prepositions and conjunctions sometimes overlap with other word classes.

English has roughly 170,000-200,000 words in current use, yet about 7% of all written English text consists of just 100 words, and 14% consists of just 250 words — many of these high-frequency words are function words (articles, prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns) rather than content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives).

Parts of speech are tested extensively in NEB exams through gap-filling, error correction, and transformation exercises. Mastering these concepts is essential for scoring well in the grammar section of both the written and objective papers.

The distinction between countable and uncountable nouns is particularly challenging for Nepali-speaking students, as Nepali does not make the same grammatical distinction. Words like 'information', 'advice', 'furniture', and 'luggage' are uncountable in English but often treated as countable in Nepali.

Modal verbs are unique to Germanic languages like English. Most other languages express modal meanings through separate lexical verbs, particles, or contextual implication rather than a dedicated grammatical category.
